title: KML Path Length: Distance of a Drawn Path
description: Measure the length of paths drawn in a KML file with the KML Path Length tool — LineString geometry summed locally, point by point. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a four-point riverside path in a KML — segments of 0.739, 0.838 and 0.794 km along the Thames — totals 2.371 km of drawn geometry, computed from the file's own coordinates.
quick_answer: The KML Path Length tool reads a KML file locally, extracts its LineString paths and sums the great-circle distance between consecutive coordinates, in kilometres and miles. Drop the file and read how long the drawn paths really are — from the geometry itself, not the file's description of it.

body.t: A walking site claims 14 km; the file's LineString sums to 11.8. Believe the geometry — descriptions outlive edits, coordinates do not lie politely. The GPX sibling is the
Someone drew the route in Google Earth and sent the KML. Its length prices the day before the day prices you.
Cable runs, fence lines and patrol paths stored as KML get budget-grade lengths from their drawn geometry.
Two KMLs, two variants of a course — lengths side by side settle the 'shorter option' argument with arithmetic.

Four points from Westminster downstream: hops of 0.739 + 0.838 + 0.794 km = 2.371 km. KML stores coordinates as lon,lat — the tool reads them in KML's own order, which is the bug this example exists to pre-empt in your own scripts.
A hand-drawn path cuts every corner its author smoothed with the mouse — drawn lengths run a few percent under walked truth on winding ground, the same chord bias as sparse GPS, in a cheaper suit.

popular_table.note: Altitude in the tuples is ignored for length: the measurement is surface distance, like the GPX tools — a 10% grade adds only ~0.5% of true slope distance.

faq: Ring geometry is measurable and reported as perimeter where the file's structure presents it; open LineStrings are the primary path case. Points contribute nothing, correctly.

Really: KML's tuple order is longitude,latitude[,altitude] — the reverse of GPX and of everyday speech. The tool parses KML's convention natively; most hand-rolled scripts that get KML wrong, get this wrong.
Drawn in Google Earth versus recorded by GPS?
Both are polylines to this tool. Drawn paths carry the corner-smoothing bias; recorded dense tracks carry almost none — the number is the file's, the interpretation is yours.
A LineString whose last tuple returns to its first closes the loop in the sum. An unclosed 'loop' measures open — check the file if the total feels one leg short.
Does it follow roads or paths on the ground?
No — straight hops between the file's tuples, the geometry as drawn. Snapping to a path network is a routing engine's job.
Haversine hops are great-circle segments — a transcontinental LineString sums as the sphere dictates, which is the correct behaviour for a straight-line file.
They sum to zero, reported as such — a degenerate path is a finding, not a failure.
